lesson_title: Why Pylons Are Full of Holes
hook_text: A forty-metre steel tower that is mostly air. Here is why the gaps make it stronger.
clip_script: Those steel towers along the highway hold power cables for fifty years, through every storm, and they are mostly empty space. Why? Because in a solid post, most of the steel does nothing. The loads run down the four corner legs, so engineers keep the legs and throw away the rest. Less steel, less weight, and the wind blows straight through. But a frame of rectangles folds. Push one corner and it racks sideways. So every panel gets an X: two diagonals, four triangles, and triangles cannot fold. When the wind hits, one diagonal stretches and the other squashes, and together they hold the panel square. The X also grips the long legs every metre so they cannot bow. Wide base at the bottom so it cannot tip. Stiff from the triangles, stable from the base. Your cardboard frame needs exactly the same two things.
visual_style: Whiteboard solid post fades to four corner legs; rectangles rack and then X-braces snap in and lock them; a wind arrow stretches one diagonal and squashes the other; the base widens.
pacing: Why open, why X, tension and compression, base, and the link to the model.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and count the triangles in one panel of the next pylon you pass.
